about: Galecto is a Copenhagen-based clinical-stage biotechnology company, listed on Nasdaq (GLTO), that developed treatments for fibrosis and cancer, including galectin inhibitors and later mutant calreticulin antibodies for myeloproliferative neoplasms. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness and limited sponsorship capacity.

about: LegoChem Biosciences is a South Korean biotech based in Daejeon that develops antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) using its proprietary ConjuAll platform, and has signed licensing deals worth billions of dollars with global pharma companies. It is listed on KOSDAQ (141080). Customers are pharma partners rather than patients, and revenue comes from licensing and milestones. The funding shown is in won. It is a B2B drug developer with no consumer brand awareness.

Swedish Orphan Biovitrum (Sobi) is a Stockholm-based biopharmaceutical company focused on rare diseases, with products such as Kineret, Doptelet, Aspaveli, Gamifant and Altuviiio for haemophilia. It is listed on Nasdaq Stockholm (SOBI) and sells to hospitals and specialists in Europe, the US and other regions, with revenue of over SEK 25 billion. It acquired CTI BioPharma in 2023. It is a B2B pharma brand known to physicians, not consumers.

UPM Sappi Graphic Paper JV is a planned joint venture between Finland's UPM-Kymmene and South Africa's Sappi to combine their European graphic paper businesses, such as magazine and catalogue papers, to cope with falling demand. The input shows funding of 700 million, last dated May 2026. It would serve publishers, printers and merchants and is B2B, with no consumer brand profile.

about: Abcuro is a Newton, Massachusetts biotechnology company developing ulviprubart (KLRG1-targeting antibody), a candidate for inclusion body myositis, a rare muscle disease, and other T-cell mediated conditions. It is a private clinical-stage company funded by venture capital and has no approved product. It is a drug developer, with no consumer brand awareness and few commercial resources for sponsorship. Customers would eventually be neurologists and patients.

Agenus is a Lexington, Massachusetts biotechnology company developing immuno-oncology treatments such as botensilimab and balstilimab, plus vaccine adjuvants like QS-21 Stimulon. It is listed on Nasdaq (AGEN) and earns revenue from partnerships, such as with Gilead, and royalties. It has no widely marketed product yet. It is a B2B science company with low consumer brand awareness. It is based in the Boston area and has research and manufacturing facilities there.

Alpha Compute Corp. is described in the input as a company operating as a digital asset treasury, based in Dover, Delaware, and categorised under biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, which suggests a repurposed or rebranded shell. The input shows funding of about $540 million, last dated April 2026. It is a financial and crypto-oriented vehicle with no consumer profile, and its business should be verified before outreach.

about: ALX Oncology is a South San Francisco clinical-stage biotechnology company developing evorpacept, a CD47-blocking therapy for cancers including gastric and head and neck cancers, in combination with other drugs. It is listed on Nasdaq (ALXO), has no approved product and funds itself through equity. It is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Its revenue is minimal and it depends on equity raises and collaborations to fund trials.

Aquestive Therapeutics is a Warren, New Jersey specialty pharmaceutical company that makes oral film drug delivery products, including Libervant for seizures and the Anaphylm epinephrine film candidate for allergic reactions, and receives royalties on others such as Suboxone film. It is listed on Nasdaq (AQST). Customers are pharmacies, patients and partner pharma firms. It is a small company with low consumer awareness.

Artiva Biotherapeutics is a San Diego clinical-stage biotech developing natural killer cell therapies off the shelf, such as AlloNK, for autoimmune diseases and cancers. It was listed on Nasdaq (ARTV) in 2024 and works with partners like Merck. It has no approved products and earns revenue from collaborations. It is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Its customers would eventually be hospitals and patients, and it is based in California.

ASP Isotopes is a Dallas-based company that develops isotope enrichment technology, such as aerodynamic separation, for producing medical, nuclear and other isotopes, with a focus on Mo-100, Yb-176 and Lithium-6, and with activity in South Africa. It is listed on Nasdaq (ASPI) and also spun out Quantum Leap Energy. It sells to pharmaceutical, nuclear fuel and semiconductor customers. It is a small deep-technology B2B firm with low consumer awareness.

Avere Therapeutics is a biotechnology and health care company based in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania, according to the input. The input shows funding of about $500 million, last dated August 2026, but gives no detail on its pipeline. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

about: Axogen is a Florida medical technology company that develops nerve repair products, including Avance Nerve Graft, a processed human nerve allograft, plus nerve connectors and protectors for treating peripheral nerve injuries. It sells to surgeons and hospitals in the United States and is listed on Nasdaq (AXGN). It is a medical device company with little consumer awareness. Revenue is in the low hundreds of millions of dollars from surgeon-led procedures.

Beta Bionics is an Irvine, California medical device company that makes the iLet Bionic Pancreas, an automated insulin delivery system for people with type 1 diabetes that adjusts insulin dosing with an adaptive algorithm. It sells to patients through pharmacies and distributors and is listed on Nasdaq (BBNX) since its 2025 IPO. It has solid awareness among diabetes patients and endocrinologists, but not among the general public.

Bicara Therapeutics is a Boston clinical-stage biotech company developing ficerafusp alfa, a bifunctional antibody that targets EGFR and TGF-beta, for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. It is listed on Nasdaq (BCAX) since its 2024 IPO and has no approved product. It is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be oncologists and cancer patients, and revenue is currently zero beyond financing.

Cabaletta Bio is a Philadelphia clinical-stage biotech developing CAR-T cell therapies, such as rese-cel, aimed at resetting the immune system for autoimmune diseases like lupus and myositis. It is listed on Nasdaq (CABA), with no approved products. It is a drug developer funded by equity and has no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be hospitals and rheumatologists, and it currently has no commercial revenue.

Candel Therapeutics is a Needham, Massachusetts clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing viral immunotherapies for solid tumours, notably CAN-2409 (aglatimagene besadenovec) for prostate cancer, and CAN-3110. It is listed on Nasdaq (CADL) and has no approved products. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be cancer centres and patients, and it has no commercial revenue yet, relying on equity financing.

CellCentric is a Cambridge, UK biotechnology company developing small-molecule drugs that block the p300/CBP epigenetic proteins, such as inobrodib, for blood cancers like multiple myeloma. It is a private company backed by venture and institutional investors. It has no marketed product and is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. It has run clinical trials in the UK and elsewhere and is funded by investors.

DBV Technologies is a French biopharmaceutical company based in Chatillon near Paris, developing the Viaskin epicutaneous patch for treating food allergies such as peanut allergy in children. It is listed on Nasdaq (DBVT) and Euronext Paris and is in late-stage trials. Customers will eventually be allergists, patients and health systems. It is a drug-delivery developer with little consumer awareness. It has a presence in France and the United States, where it runs most clinical trials.

Dren Bio is a San Carlos, California biotechnology company developing antibody-based therapies that harness phagocytic cells to remove disease-causing cells and proteins, for autoimmune disease and cancer. It has signed large licensing deals with Sanofi. It is privately held and has no approved product. It is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be hospitals and patients, and revenue comes from partnership payments.

about: eGenesis is a Cambridge, Massachusetts biotechnology company that uses gene editing to engineer pig organs for transplantation into humans, known as xenotransplantation, including kidneys. A gene-edited eGenesis kidney was transplanted into a living patient in 2024 at Massachusetts General Hospital. It is private, funded by venture investors, and has no approved product. It has moderate public attention but no consumer brand.

Everest Medicines is a pharmaceutical company listed in Hong Kong (1952), focused on bringing innovative drugs to China and Asia, such as Nefecon for IgA nephropathy, Xerava, Velsipity and mRNA technology. The Crunchbase entry gives a New York location, but its operations are mainly in Shanghai and Greater China. It sells mainly to hospitals. It is a B2B pharma brand with limited consumer awareness.

about: Evommune is a Palo Alto clinical-stage biotechnology company developing therapies for chronic inflammatory diseases driven by mast cells, with lead candidates such as EVO301 and EVO756. It went public on Nasdaq (EVMN) in 2025. It has no approved product and is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be dermatologists, allergists and patients with chronic inflammatory diseases, and it has no commercial revenue yet.

GlaxoSmithKline, now GSK plc, is a London-headquartered global pharmaceutical and vaccines company, with medicines for respiratory disease, HIV (ViiV), oncology and vaccines such as Shingrix and Arexvy. Its consumer health division was demerged as Haleon in 2022. It is listed on the London and New York exchanges (GSK) with revenue of about 30 billion pounds. It sells to health systems and doctors, and its brand is globally known, with sport sponsorship history.

MannKind is a Danbury, Connecticut biopharmaceutical company that makes Afrezza, an ultra-rapid-acting inhaled insulin for adults with diabetes, and Tyvaso DPI, an inhaled treprostinil powder for pulmonary hypertension partnered with United Therapeutics. It is listed on Nasdaq (MNKD) and sells to patients through specialty pharmacies and healthcare providers. It has moderate consumer brand awareness within the diabetes community. It also earns royalties and manufacturing revenue from its partnership, and it has operations in Connecticut and California.

Merz Pharma is a family-owned German pharmaceutical group headquartered in Frankfurt, known for its aesthetics, neurotoxin and consumer health products, including Xeomin, Belotero and Ultherapy. It sells mainly to doctors and also to consumers. Founded in 1908, it is private and owned by the Merz family. Its brands are well known to aesthetic physicians, and it has some consumer recognition in Europe.

Nanobiotix is a Paris-based clinical-stage nanomedicine company developing NBTXR3, a radioenhancer injected into tumours to boost radiotherapy, with a partnership with Janssen. It is listed on Euronext Paris and Nasdaq (NBTX). It has no approved product and is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be cancer centres and patients, and revenue comes from licensing and collaboration payments rather than product sales.

Neurogene is a New York clinical-stage biotechnology company developing gene therapies for rare neurological diseases, notably NGN-401 for Rett syndrome. It is listed on Nasdaq (NGNE) following a 2023 merger with Neoleukin. It has no approved product and is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be neurologists and families affected by rare childhood disease, and it has no commercial revenue yet, relying on equity financing.

Neuronetics is a Malvern, Pennsylvania medical device company that makes the NeuroStar Advanced Therapy System, a transcranial magnetic stimulation treatment for major depression that does not use drugs or surgery. It sells devices to psychiatrists and clinics in the United States and is listed on Nasdaq (STIM). Patients see the brand through advertising for the therapy, giving moderate awareness among people with depression.

OMass Therapeutics is an Oxford, UK biotechnology company discovering small-molecule medicines for rare, immune and metabolic diseases by studying membrane proteins using its native mass spectrometry platform. It is private and backed by investors including Syncona. It has partnerships with pharma companies. It has no marketed product and no consumer brand awareness. Its customers are pharmaceutical partners and its revenue comes from collaborations.

Orca Bio is a Menlo Park, California clinical-stage cell therapy company developing Orca-T, a precision allogeneic cell therapy for patients undergoing stem cell transplants for blood cancers. It is private and venture-backed, with a late-stage trial and an FDA review of its product. It is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be transplant centres and patients with blood cancers.

ProQR Therapeutics is a Leiden, Netherlands biotechnology company developing RNA-editing medicines using its Axiomer platform, with programmes in liver and other genetic diseases, including partnerships with Eli Lilly. It is listed on Nasdaq (PRQR). It has no approved product and is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be physicians and patients, and revenue comes from collaboration payments.

Rapid Micro Biosystems is a Lexington, Massachusetts company that makes the Growth Direct system, an automated platform for quality control microbial testing used in pharmaceutical and biologic manufacturing. It sells instruments and consumables to drug makers and is listed on Nasdaq (RPID). It is a B2B life science tools company with no consumer brand awareness. Customers include large pharma and biotech manufacturers, and revenue is under US$50 million a year.

Renaissance Philanthropy is a New York-based nonprofit organisation, founded by Tom Kalil, Eric Schmidt and others, that channels philanthropic funding into science, technology and public-interest projects through advisory services, funds and prizes. It is not a company with products. The funding shown is philanthropic capital. It has a visible profile in science policy circles and none as a consumer brand.

Sail Biomedicines is a Cambridge, Massachusetts biotechnology company created by Flagship Pioneering, formerly Laronde, developing endless RNA (eRNA) technology for programming cells with circular RNA medicines. It is private and venture-backed, and has no approved product. It is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be physicians and patients, and its revenue comes from collaborations and financing rather than sales.

about: Shattuck Labs is an Austin, Texas clinical-stage biotechnology company developing biologic drugs for inflammatory diseases and cancer using its Agonist Redirected Checkpoint technology, such as SL-325 (DR3 antagonist). It is listed on Nasdaq (STTK). It has no approved products and is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be clinicians and patients, and it earns revenue from collaborations at best.

Star Therapeutics is a South San Francisco biotechnology company, whose stated mission is to develop therapies for as many patients as possible, with a focus on bleeding and clotting disorders, including its antibody VGA039 for von Willebrand disease. It is private and venture-backed. It has no approved products and is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be haematologists and patients, and it has no commercial revenue yet.

about: Trevi Therapeutics is a New Haven, Connecticut clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing Haduvio (oral nalbuphine ER) for chronic cough in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and refractory chronic cough. It is listed on Nasdaq (TRVI) and has no approved product. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be respiratory specialists and patients, and it has no commercial revenue yet, relying on equity financing for trials.

Vedanta Biosciences is a Cambridge, Massachusetts clinical-stage company developing defined bacterial consortia as oral microbiome therapies, such as VE303 for C. difficile infection, with Flagship Pioneering origins. It is private and venture-backed, and has no approved product. It is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be gastroenterologists and hospitals, and its revenue comes from collaborations and financing.

Accuray is a Madison, Wisconsin radiation oncology company that makes the CyberKnife robotic radiosurgery system and the Radixact (TomoTherapy) platform, and sells service contracts and software to hospitals and cancer centres worldwide. It is listed on Nasdaq (ARAY), with revenue of roughly US$450 million a year and a large installed base in the US, Europe, China and Japan. It is a B2B medical equipment brand, well known to oncologists but not to consumers.

Aclaris Therapeutics is a Wayne, Pennsylvania biopharmaceutical company developing immuno-inflammatory medicines, with programmes such as ATI-2138, a covalent ITK/JAK3 inhibitor, and ATI-052, a bispecific antibody. It previously sold dermatology products before divesting them. It is listed on Nasdaq (ACRS) and funds trials through equity and collaboration revenue. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be dermatologists and rheumatologists.

AdvanCell is a radiopharmaceutical company developing targeted alpha therapy for cancer using lead-212 isotope, with its roots in Australia and a presence in the United States, listed in the input at Boston. It builds isotope generators and supply, plus drug candidates, with trials in prostate cancer. It is privately held and venture-backed, and has no approved product. It is a B2B drug developer with no consumer brand awareness.

It is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness.

about: BioAge Labs is an Emeryville, California clinical-stage biotechnology company that uses human ageing and metabolic biology data to develop drugs for obesity and age-related diseases, with candidates such as BGE-102, an NLRP3 inhibitor. It is listed on Nasdaq (BIOA) and its azelaprag programme was stopped in 2024 after safety findings. It has no approved product and is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness.

Celularity is a Florham Park, New Jersey cell therapy and regenerative medicine company that derives cell and biomaterial products from the placenta, including cell therapies for cancer and degenerative conditions, plus commercial products sold to wound care and surgical customers. It is listed on Nasdaq (CELU), after a 2021 SPAC merger. It is a small B2B biotech with no consumer brand awareness.

Climb Bio is a Wellesley, Massachusetts clinical-stage biotechnology company developing budoprutug, an anti-CD19 antibody for autoimmune kidney disease such as membranous nephropathy, and other immune therapies. It was formerly named Eliem Therapeutics and was renamed in 2024, and is listed on Nasdaq (CLYM). It has no approved product and no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be nephrologists and patients.

Corvus Pharmaceuticals is a Burlingame, California clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing soquelitinib, an ITK inhibitor, for T-cell lymphoma and atopic dermatitis. It is listed on Nasdaq (CRVS) and has no approved product. It earns no product revenue and relies on equity raises. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be oncologists, dermatologists and patients, and the company is based near San Francisco.

CORXEL Pharmaceuticals is a Berkeley Heights, New Jersey biotechnology company, with Chinese roots, developing metabolic medicines, notably an oral GLP-1 drug candidate for obesity and diabetes. It is privately held and backed by investors. It has no approved product, so it is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be physicians and patients managing weight and diabetes.

about: Emergent BioSolutions is a Gaithersburg, Maryland biopharmaceutical company that makes medical countermeasures such as the BioThrax and Cyfendus anthrax vaccines, ACAM2000 smallpox vaccine and Narcan nasal spray for opioid overdose. Its main customers are the US government and public health agencies. Listed on the NYSE (EBS), it grew through acquisitions but ran into manufacturing problems with COVID-19 vaccine contract work. Narcan is a consumer-visible product, but the corporate brand is mostly known in healthcare.

enGene is a clinical-stage biotechnology company working on non-viral gene therapy for bladder cancer, with a lead candidate detalimogene voraplasmid, delivered into the bladder. It is listed on Nasdaq (ENGN) and based in Boston and Montreal. It has no approved product and funds trials through equity. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be urologists and patients.

Immix Biopharma is a Los Angeles clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing NXC-201, a CAR-T cell therapy for relapsed or refractory AL amyloidosis, a rare blood disease. It is listed on Nasdaq (IMMX) and has no approved product. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be haematologists and transplant centres, and revenue is zero beyond financing. It is a development-stage company funded by equity raises.

Jasper Therapeutics is a Redwood City, California clinical-stage biotechnology company developing briquilimab, an anti-KIT antibody for mast-cell diseases such as chronic spontaneous urticaria and for stem cell transplant conditioning. It is listed on Nasdaq (JSPR) and has no approved product. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be haematologists, allergists and transplant centres, with no commercial revenue.

LB Pharmaceuticals is a New York clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing LB-102, an N-methyl derivative of amisulpride, as a treatment for schizophrenia and other psychiatric conditions. It listed on Nasdaq (LBRX) in 2025. It has no approved product and is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be psychiatrists and patients, and the company has no commercial revenue, relying on its IPO proceeds and investor funding.

Lisata Therapeutics is a Basking Ridge, New Jersey clinical-stage pharmaceutical company, formerly Caladrius Biosciences, developing certepetide (LSTA1), a tumour-penetrating peptide used with chemotherapy in pancreatic and other solid cancers. It is listed on Nasdaq (LSTA). It has no approved product and no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be oncologists and cancer centres, and it has no commercial revenue, relying on equity financing and partnerships. It is a very small company.

Medipost is a stem cell therapy company, headquartered in South Korea and listed on KOSDAQ, best known for Cartistem, an umbilical cord blood-derived stem cell treatment for knee cartilage defects, with a US presence in the Boston area shown in the input. It sells to hospitals and orthopaedic surgeons. It is a B2B biotech with limited consumer brand awareness. Its parent business is mostly in Korea.

about: MeiraGTx is a gene therapy company with offices in New York and London, developing AAV treatments for inherited eye diseases, hearing loss and Parkinson's disease, including a collaboration with Janssen on retinal disease and a manufacturing facility in the UK. It is listed on Nasdaq (MGTX). It has no approved product in its own name, so it is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness.

Ocugen is a Malvern, Pennsylvania clinical-stage biotechnology company developing OCU400, a modifier gene therapy for retinitis pigmentosa, along with other eye and vaccine programmes. It was the US partner for Bharat Biotech's Covaxin COVID-19 vaccine. It is listed on Nasdaq (OCGN) and has no approved product of its own. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness.

Ollin Biosciences is an ophthalmology biotechnology company, listed in the input in Austin, Texas, developing therapies for eye diseases such as wet age-related macular degeneration and diabetic eye disease. It is privately held and venture-backed. It has no approved product, and the input offers no further detail. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. (Limited public information - check before outreach.)

about: Orchestra BioMed is a New Hope, Pennsylvania biomedical innovation company that develops devices through partnerships, including BackBeat Cardiac Neuromodulation Therapy with Medtronic for hypertension and the Virtue sirolimus-eluting balloon with Terumo. It is listed on Nasdaq (OBIO) and earns revenue from partners. It is a small B2B medtech with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would be cardiologists and hospitals once devices are approved.

Oricell Therapeutics is a Shanghai-based Chinese cell therapy company developing CAR-T and related immune cell treatments for blood cancers, solid tumours and autoimmune diseases. It is privately held and funded by venture and strategic investors. It has no approved product yet. It is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness and limited visibility outside China. Customers would eventually be hospitals.

about: Outlook Therapeutics is an Iselin, New Jersey ophthalmic biopharmaceutical company that developed ONS-5010 (bevacizumab-vikg, Lytenava), an on-label bevacizumab injection for wet age-related macular degeneration, which has been through repeated FDA review cycles. It is listed on Nasdaq (OTLK). It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be retina specialists and patients, and it has no meaningful revenue, relying on equity financing to fund its regulatory efforts.

Perspective Therapeutics is a Seattle radiopharmaceutical company developing targeted lead-212 alpha therapies and imaging agents for cancers, including VMT-alpha-NET for neuroendocrine tumours and VMT01 for melanoma. It is listed on NYSE American (CATX) and has no approved product. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be oncologists and cancer centres, and it has no commercial revenue, relying on equity financing and manufacturing partnerships.

Pyxis Oncology is a Boston clinical-stage oncology company developing micvotabart pelidotin, an antibody-drug conjugate targeting EDB+FN for solid tumours, including head and neck cancer. It is listed on Nasdaq (PYXS) and has no approved product. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be oncologists and cancer centres, and it has no commercial revenue, relying on equity financing and licensing royalties from a legacy asset.

Q32 Bio is a Waltham, Massachusetts clinical-stage biotechnology company developing immune therapies for autoimmune disease, led by bempikibart, an antibody targeting IL-7R alpha. It is listed on Nasdaq (QTTB) and has no approved product. It is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be rheumatologists and dermatologists, and it has no commercial revenue, relying on equity financing and prior pharma partnerships.

ReCode Therapeutics is a genetic medicines company, shown in Dallas, developing lipid nanoparticle delivery of RNA and gene editing therapies for inherited lung diseases such as cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia. It is privately held and venture-backed. It has no approved product, so it is a drug developer with no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be pulmonologists and patients.

about: SAB Biotherapeutics is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company, now centred in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, that uses genetically engineered cattle to produce fully human polyclonal antibodies, with programmes in diabetes and infectious disease. It is listed on Nasdaq (SABS) after a SPAC merger in 2021. It has no approved product and is a small drug developer with no consumer brand awareness.

Science Corporation is an Alameda, California neurotechnology company founded by Max Hodak, former Neuralink president, developing brain-computer interfaces and the PRIMA retinal implant for vision loss, whose assets it acquired from Pixium Vision. It is privately funded by investors. It sells to clinicians and hospitals and is an early stage medtech brand with strong media attention but no mass consumer reach.

Shionogi is a Japanese pharmaceutical company based in Osaka, founded in 1878, whose products include the influenza drug Xofluza, the antibiotic cefiderocol (Fetroja) and the HIV drug dolutegravir via ViiV. It also developed the COVID-19 antiviral Xocova. It is listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange (4507) with revenue of several hundred billion yen. It sells to doctors and hospitals, and has some consumer recognition in Japan.

Silence Therapeutics is a London-based RNA interference (siRNA) biotechnology company, listed on Nasdaq (SLN), developing medicines such as zerlasiran for high lipoprotein(a) cardiovascular risk and divesiran for polycythemia vera, with partnerships with AstraZeneca, Novartis and Mallinckrodt. It has no approved product and no consumer brand awareness. Revenue comes from collaboration payments, and customers would eventually be cardiologists and haematologists. Its customers would eventually be hospitals and specialists.

Teva Pharmaceuticals USA is the United States arm of Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, the Israel-founded world leader in generics, with brands including Copaxone, Austedo, Ajovy and Uzedy. Its US operations are based in North Wales, Pennsylvania. Teva is listed on the NYSE (TEVA) and has annual revenue of about US$16 billion. It sells to pharmacies, hospitals and health systems, and is widely seen as a generics supplier, though consumers rarely see the Teva name.

Tidal Vision is a Bellingham, Washington materials company that converts crustacean shells, from crab and shrimp, into chitosan-based biomolecules for water treatment, agriculture and textile applications. It sells to industrial and agricultural customers and operates a manufacturing plant in Washington. It is privately held and venture-backed, a sustainability-oriented B2B business with limited consumer brand awareness. Its products are used in industrial inputs.

It is listed on Nasdaq (WHWK). It has no approved product of its own beyond legacy assets, and no consumer brand awareness. Customers would eventually be oncologists and cancer centres, and it has no commercial revenue to speak of.

about: Chinese traditional medicine and pharmaceutical group headquartered in Tianjin, best known for Compound Danshen Dripping Pills, a cardiovascular medicine with global clinical trials, as well as other herbal injectables and capsules. Tasly Pharmaceutical is listed in Shanghai (600535) and part of Tasly Holding Group, selling to hospitals, pharmacies and exporting to Russia, Southeast Asia and elsewhere. Revenue runs into billions of yuan. Brand is well recognised in China's health market, with sponsorship activity in sport and TV, and little profile in Western markets.

Consumer genetics company that sold home saliva DNA kits for ancestry reports and health risk insights, and ran a drug research arm that developed therapies from its genetic database of millions of customers. Founded in 2006 in California, it listed on Nasdaq (ME) through a SPAC in 2021 at a valuation of about 3.5 billion dollars. After sales fell and a 2023 data breach, it filed for Chapter 11 in 2025 and its assets were bought by TTAM Research Institute, led by co-founder Anne Wojcicki. Well-known consumer brand in the US and UK.

Biotechnology research company launched in 2022 with 3 billion dollars of private funding, built around cellular rejuvenation and reprogramming, the idea that cells can be reset to reverse disease and aging damage. Its scientists include Nobel laureate Shinya Yamanaka and it is led by former Roche executive Hal Barron, with institutes in California, San Diego, Cambridge UK and Japan. Backers reportedly include Yuri Milner and Jeff Bezos. No products yet. High media profile but no consumer brand.

South African pharmaceutical group, listed on the JSE (APN), that makes and sells branded and generic medicines, hospital products such as anaesthetics, and the Fraxiparine thrombosis drug, across over 150 countries. Customers are hospitals, pharmacies, governments and wholesalers; it also does vaccine manufacturing and fill-finish work in Gqeberha. Annual revenue is in the tens of billions of rand and it has major sites in South Africa, Europe and Latin America. Respected within healthcare, with limited consumer awareness.

Global oncology company, renamed BeOne Medicines in 2025 and domiciled in Switzerland, with big operations in China and the US. Its main medicines are Brukinsa (zanubrutinib) for blood cancers and Tevimbra (tislelizumab) for solid tumours, sold to hospitals and health systems in more than 70 markets. Founded in 2010 by John Oyler and Xiaodong Wang and listed on Nasdaq, Hong Kong and Shanghai. Large drug maker, mostly known to clinicians and investors rather than the public.

Swiss healthcare group in Basel and one of the world's biggest drug and diagnostics companies, with its Genentech unit in the US and Chugai in Japan. Key medicines include Ocrevus, Hemlibra, Tecentriq, Herceptin and Avastin, while its diagnostics unit sells lab analyzers, glucose monitors and tests. Customers are hospitals, labs, health systems and payers, and sales are over 60 billion Swiss francs. Employs roughly 100,000 people and is a recognised corporate name, though sold to professionals rather than consumers.

US precision medicine biotech in Cambridge, Massachusetts, that developed kinase inhibitors for rare cancers and blood disorders, led by Ayvakit (avapritinib) for gastrointestinal stromal tumours and systemic mastocytosis, and Gavreto for thyroid and lung cancer. Sold to specialist physicians and hospitals. Previously Nasdaq-listed, it agreed to be acquired by Sanofi in 2025 for about 9.5 billion dollars. Known mainly to oncologists and investors.

US biotechnology company in Cambridge, Massachusetts, focused on neurology and neuroscience. Its products include multiple sclerosis drugs such as Tecfidera, Vumerity and Tysabri, the spinal muscular atrophy treatment Spinraza, and Leqembi for Alzheimer's disease, developed with Eisai. Customers are hospitals, neurologists and payers worldwide, and it also earns royalties from partner products. Founded in 1978 and listed on Nasdaq (BIIB). Strong healthcare brand among doctors and patients.

US cell and gene therapy technology company that provides a development platform and large-scale cell manufacturing site (BaseCamp) in Waltham, Massachusetts, and also incubates its own spinout companies, including Life Edit for gene editing. It serves biotech and pharma partners through development and manufacturing contracts and works on cancer and inflammatory disease treatments. Founded in 2017 and backed by very large private funding rounds. Known mainly inside the biotech industry, with no consumer brand.

about: US biopharmaceutical company that developed KarXT, later approved as Cobenfy, a new type of muscarinic drug for schizophrenia. Based in Boston, it was acquired by Bristol Myers Squibb in 2024 for about 14 billion dollars. Before that it traded on Nasdaq (KRTX) and was a high-profile clinical-stage name. Its customers will be psychiatrists and health systems under the new owner, and it has no consumer brand.

US genetic testing company in Austin, Texas, specialising in cell-free DNA tests: Panorama for prenatal screening, Signatera for cancer recurrence monitoring and Prospera for transplant rejection. It sells to doctors, hospitals and health systems and bills insurers, with millions of tests run each year and revenues over a billion dollars. Listed on Nasdaq (NTRA). Well known among clinicians and pregnant patients but a low-profile consumer brand.

US life sciences supplier based in Waltham, Massachusetts, making bioprocessing products used to produce biologic drugs: filtration systems, chromatography columns and resins, Protein A ligands and process analytics. Customers are biopharmaceutical companies and contract manufacturers, with sales through direct and distributor channels worldwide. Listed on Nasdaq (RGEN) and a long-standing supplier to the industry. Entirely business-to-business, with no consumer visibility.

Chinese synthetic biology company in Shanghai that produces long-chain dicarboxylic acids and bio-based polyamide (nylon) materials by fermentation, supplying chemical, plastics, coatings, textile and automotive customers. Revenue comes from industrial chemical sales within China and exports. Listed on Shanghai's STAR Market and linked to the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the China Merchants group. Business-to-business materials supplier with no consumer brand.

about: US cancer drug developer in Waltham, Massachusetts, whose products were Qinlock (ripretinib) for gastrointestinal stromal tumours and Romvimza (vimseltinib) for tenosynovial giant cell tumours, both sold to oncologists and hospitals. It was formerly Nasdaq-listed (DCPH) and was acquired by Ono Pharmaceutical of Japan in 2025 for about 2.4 billion dollars. Little public brand awareness outside specialist oncology and biotech investor circles.

Israeli medical device company that makes Exablate Neuro, an MR-guided focused ultrasound system which non-invasively treats essential tremor, Parkinson's tremor and other brain conditions without incision. Customers are hospitals and neurosurgery centres in dozens of countries, with revenue from systems sales and procedure-related services. Backed by investors including GE Healthcare and Koch-linked groups, it also works with partners on cancer and Alzheimer's research. Mostly known among neurologists.

US rare tumour drug developer whose products are Ogsiveo (nirogacestat) for desmoid tumours and Gomekli (mirdametinib) for neurofibromatosis type 1 plexiform neurofibromas. Customers are specialist physicians, hospitals and payers. It traded on Nasdaq (SWTX) and was acquired by Merck KGaA of Germany in 2025 for about 3.9 billion dollars. Known mainly to oncologists and investors rather than the general public.

US gene therapy company focused on eye disease, mainly wet age-related macular degeneration through its candidate ixo-vec, delivered by single injection to replace regular eye injections. It has no marketed product, so revenue depends on collaborations and capital raises. Nasdaq-listed (ADVM), and reported in 2025 to be agreeing to an acquisition by Eli Lilly. Specialist biotech name known to retina doctors and healthcare investors, with no consumer visibility.

about: US dermatology company that sells Zoryve (roflumilast) topical cream, foam and solution for plaque psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis and atopic dermatitis, approved without steroids and now extended to infants and children. Customers are dermatologists, pharmacies and payers; revenue is growing rapidly. Nasdaq-listed (ARQT) and based in Westlake Village, California. Known to doctors and, through direct-to-consumer advertising, to some patients. Competes with generic topical steroids and other dermatology brands.

US clinical-stage cancer drug company whose lead candidate is furmonertinib, an EGFR inhibitor tested in non-small cell lung cancer with certain mutations, licensed from Shanghai Allist. Listed on Nasdaq (AVBP) after a 2024 IPO and run from Pennsylvania. It has no commercial product so earns no sales and relies on investor funding. Mostly known among oncology specialists and biotech investors.

about: US biotech company in San Diego, formerly Samumed, that developed drugs targeting the Wnt pathway, led by lorecivivint, an injected treatment for knee osteoarthritis tested in late-stage trials. It also runs programs in degenerative disc disease, tendon and hair conditions. Privately held with large funding rounds from private investors, it has no product on the market. Known mostly in biotech circles.

US biopharmaceutical company in Brisbane, California, that markets Ojemda (tovorafenib), approved in 2024 for children with relapsed low-grade glioma, a brain tumour, and has licensed Ojemda rights outside the US to Ipsen. It sells to paediatric oncologists and hospitals and is Nasdaq-listed (DAWN). Founded in 2018 with a focus on rare paediatric cancers. Known to specialists and investors rather than consumers.

about: US life sciences tools company in Seattle that sold spatial biology and gene-expression instruments, notably GeoMx and CosMx spatial platforms and the nCounter system, used by academic labs and pharma researchers. It filed for Chapter 11 in February 2024 and its assets were purchased by Bruker, which completed the acquisition later that year. Previously Nasdaq-listed (NSTG), it is now a Bruker business with no separate consumer profile.

US food technology company that uses microflora fermentation to make animal-free whey and casein dairy proteins, selling them to food brands and operating consumer lines such as Brave Robot ice cream and Bored Cow milk. Customers include Nestle, Unilever and other food makers and its partner Leprino. Founded in 2014 by Ryan Pandya and Perumal Gandhi, based in Berkeley, it faced a cash crunch in 2023 and restructured. Some consumer brand awareness among sustainable-food shoppers.

US chemical company that makes chemicals through its Bioforge enzymatic and metal catalyst process, producing hydrogen peroxide, organic acids, and plant-based chemicals used in water treatment, construction, cleaning, agriculture and consumer products. Customers are industrial chemical buyers. Based in Houston and building a large Minnesota plant backed by a Department of Energy loan guarantee. Founded in 2016 by Gaurab Chakrabarti and Sean Blake. B2B profile without consumer brand.

US biotech in Pasadena, California, known for its XmAb antibody engineering platform that creates bispecific and other modified antibodies for cancer and autoimmune disease. Revenue comes from licensing partnerships and royalties on products such as Monjuvi (tafasitamab) and Alexion's Ultomiris, which uses its Xtend technology, with partners including Novartis and Vir, while it advances its own pipeline. Nasdaq-listed (XNCR). Known to biotech investors and specialist doctors, not the public.

US specialty pharmaceutical company that makes branded and generic drugs, led by Purified Cortrophin Gel for inflammatory conditions and the blood pressure drug Inderal, plus a large portfolio of generic oral and controlled-substance medicines. Its plants are in Baudette, Minnesota and East Windsor, New Jersey, selling to wholesalers, pharmacies and hospitals. Nasdaq-listed (ANIP). Modest public profile, known mostly to physicians and pharmacy buyers.

US cell therapy company building programmable T cells for solid tumours by combining CRISPR gene editing with synthetic biology and AI-designed circuits, so that engineered cells can sense and attack cancer. It runs clinical trials of its lead candidates and has partnered with larger drug firms. Privately held, with large venture and pharma-linked financing, and no commercial product yet. Known in biotech but with no consumer visibility.

about: US clinical-stage biotech developing navenibart (STAR-0215), a long-acting antibody given by injection every few months to prevent attacks of hereditary angioedema, a rare genetic disorder causing painful swelling. It earns no product revenue and relies on investors and possible partnerships to fund late-stage trials. Nasdaq-listed (ATXS), run from Boston, and followed mostly by specialist investors and allergy physicians. No public brand profile, so awareness outside healthcare is essentially nil.

US biotechnology company developing heart failure and cardiovascular drugs, with a focus on oral small molecules such as a PDE9 inhibitor intended for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, plus gene-based approaches. Formed with backing from large investors and a Takeda collaboration, it has no marketed product. Customers would be cardiologists and health systems. Private, specialist-oriented biotech with no consumer brand.

about: US late-stage cancer company developing cretostimogene grenadenorepvec, an oncolytic virus therapy delivered directly into the bladder for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, with pivotal trial results reported in recent years. It has no marketed drug yet and is funded by investors and a 2024 Nasdaq IPO (CGON). Customers would be urologists and hospitals. Operating bases in Irvine, California and Dallas. Known mostly to urology specialists and biotech investors, with no consumer visibility.

about: US biopharmaceutical company that developed dordaviprone (ONC201), a drug for H3 K27M-mutant diffuse glioma, a deadly brain tumour affecting children and young adults, after selling its smallpox antiviral Tembexa to Emergent BioSolutions. It was Nasdaq-listed (CMRX), based in Durham, North Carolina, and was acquired by Jazz Pharmaceuticals in 2025 for about 935 million dollars. Known mainly to neuro-oncologists and biotech investors; no consumer brand.

US biotech, formerly Cullinan Oncology, developing targeted cancer medicines including zipalertinib, an EGFR exon 20 inhibitor partnered with Taiho Oncology for lung cancer, and T-cell engagers for autoimmune disease. Customers would be oncologists and hospitals, with funding from investors and partner milestones rather than product sales. Nasdaq-listed (CGEM) and run from Cambridge, Massachusetts. Little public brand profile beyond biotech investors and specialist oncologists.

about: US biotech that developed personalised cancer vaccines and infectious disease vaccines based on self-amplifying RNA, with partners such as Gilead and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. It had no approved product and, after clinical and financial setbacks, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in late 2024 and sold its assets. Previously Nasdaq-listed (GRTS). No consumer brand and no remaining sponsorship capacity.

about: US biotech and medical products company that makes placental and amniotic tissue-based products for wound care, surgical recovery and sports medicine, sold under names such as EPIFIX, EPICORD and AMNIOFIX. Customers are hospitals, wound care centres, physician practices and the US military, with revenue of several hundred million dollars from product sales. Nasdaq-listed (MDXG) and based in Marietta, Georgia. Known to clinicians; not a consumer brand.

US clinical-stage neuroscience company developing navacaprant, a kappa opioid receptor antagonist tested for major depressive disorder, and other drugs for psychiatric and neurological disease. It has no marketed product and is funded by investors after a 2023 Nasdaq IPO (NMRA), one of the larger biotech listings that year. Customers would be psychiatrists and health systems. Unknown to the general public, with a profile limited to biotech investors and brain-disease researchers.

about: US cell therapy company developing off-the-shelf natural killer (NK) cell treatments derived from donors and engineered to attack B-cell cancers and autoimmune diseases such as lupus. It has no approved product and funds its work through equity raises and partnerships. Nasdaq-listed (NKTX) with research and manufacturing in the San Francisco Bay Area. Known to biotech investors and specialist clinicians only, with no consumer awareness.

about: US specialty pharmaceutical company that sells Xhance, a fluticasone nasal spray delivered with a patented exhalation system to treat chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps. Customers are ENT specialists and allergists who prescribe it, and sales run through pharmacies and insurers in the United States. Nasdaq-listed (OPTN) and based in Yardley, Pennsylvania. Small drug firm with prescriber-focused marketing and moderate patient awareness.

about: US regenerative medicine company that makes bioactive wound care and surgical biologics, including Apligraf and Dermagraft living cell skin products and the PuraPly antimicrobial matrix, used on diabetic foot ulcers and venous leg ulcers. It sells to wound care clinics, hospitals and physicians and relies on Medicare reimbursement. Nasdaq-listed (ORGO) with its home base in Canton, Massachusetts. Specialist medical brand, little consumer awareness.

US pharmaceutical company that sells Olinvyk (oliceridine), an intravenous opioid painkiller approved by the FDA in 2020 for acute pain in hospitals, and has other pain and neurology candidates in development. Customers are hospitals, surgical centres and anaesthesiologists. Nasdaq-listed (TRVN), based in King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, with limited commercial traction and a small team. Known mostly to hospital pharmacists and pain specialists, with no consumer brand.

about: US clinical-stage biotech developing oral antiviral drugs for chronic hepatitis B, plus candidates for MASH (fatty liver disease) and coronaviruses. It has no product on sale and relies on equity raises and collaborations with larger pharmaceutical firms to fund trials. Nasdaq-listed (ALGS) and based in South San Francisco, California. Little public profile outside biotech, and customers would eventually be liver specialists and health systems.

about: US biotech pioneering PROTAC protein degraders, drugs that mark disease-causing proteins for destruction by the cell. Its lead is vepdegestrant for breast cancer, co-developed with Pfizer, alongside programs for prostate cancer and neurology, with collaborations including Novartis and Genentech. Based in New Haven, Connecticut, and Nasdaq-listed (ARVN). Customers would be oncologists and hospitals; known to investors and scientists, not to consumers.

Chinese-American clinical-stage cancer company developing drugs for hard-to-treat blood cancers, including olverembatinib and lisaftoclax (a BCL-2 inhibitor), with its base in Suzhou and a US presence in Rockville, Maryland. Revenue comes from sales in China and partnerships with firms such as Takeda. Listed on Nasdaq (AAPG) and the Hong Kong exchange. Known to haematologists and healthcare investors, with no consumer awareness.

about: US biotech spun out of BridgeBio, developing small molecule cancer drugs aimed at RAS-driven tumours, including pan-KRAS and RAS-PI3K breaker programs in early clinical trials. Became public in 2025 through a merger with a SPAC, trading on Nasdaq (BBOT), having raised a large private round beforehand. No product revenue yet, as customers would be oncologists. Known to biotech investors and specialist researchers rather than consumers.

about: US clinical-stage cancer company in Boston developing antibody therapies, led by tovecimig (CTX-009), a bispecific antibody aimed at biliary tract cancer, plus others for solid tumours. Trial funding comes from equity raises and licensing arrangements with Asian drug makers. Nasdaq-listed (CMPX). It has no marketed product, and its profile is limited to oncology specialists and biotech investors; there is no consumer brand awareness to speak of.

about: International pharmaceutical compounding company that supplies raw materials, sterile and non-sterile preparations, and personalised medicine services to pharmacies, hospitals and clinics, with sales across Europe, Latin America, the US and other regions. Customers are compounding pharmacists and healthcare providers in around 30 countries. Listed on Euronext Brussels (FAGR), with Belgian roots and management bases in the Netherlands. Professional healthcare supplier with little consumer exposure.

Visible to eye care professionals and some pharma investors, with little direct consumer brand awareness.
